title: Chapter 2 (General Section): Underwriting and Rate Making

cards.title: What is Underwriting?
cards.content: Underwriting is the process of determining: (1) WHETHER the risk offered for insurance is ACCEPTABLE, and (2) If yes, at what RATE, TERMS and CONDITIONS the insurance cover will be provided. The officer who performs this entire process is called an UNDERWRITER.

cards.title: Risk Classification in Underwriting
cards.content: During underwriting, risks are CLASSIFIED into different categories. The process of classifying risk and deciding which category it falls into is of great importance for RATE MAKING — it directly determines what premium will be charged.

cards.title: What is Rate?
cards.content: RATE is the price of a given unit of insurance. It is the cost charged per unit of insurance coverage. Premium = Sum Insured × Rate.

cards.title: Basic Objective of Rate Making
cards.content: The BASIC OBJECTIVE of the rate making process is to ensure that the price of insurance is ADEQUATE and REASONABLE — meaning the price charged should be correct, fair, and justified. Not too high, not too low.

cards.title: Sum Insured
cards.content: SUM INSURED is the MAXIMUM AMOUNT that an insurance company will INDEMNIFY (pay) as per the policy conditions. It is the upper ceiling on the insurer's liability. Example: If Sum Insured = Rs. 10 lakh, the insurer will never pay more than Rs. 10 lakh regardless of the actual loss.

cards.title: Pure Premium — How It Grows
cards.content: Pure Premium is the base premium calculated to cover expected losses. It is then LOADED — a percentage is added to provide for: (1) Expenses, (2) Reserves, and (3) Profits. After adding these, pure premium becomes the FINAL PREMIUM.

cards.title: What is a Hazard?
cards.content: In insurance, HAZARD refers to conditions that CREATE and INCREASE the chance of loss. A hazard is a factor that either increases the FREQUENCY of loss (how often it occurs) or the SEVERITY/IMPACT of loss (how much damage is caused) — or BOTH.

cards.title: Physical Hazard
cards.content: PHYSICAL HAZARD is a tangible, observable condition that affects the probability or severity of loss. Key exam fact: Physical Hazard CAN BE ASCERTAINED from the information given in the PROPOSAL FORM. It is not unknown — it can be identified and assessed.

cards.title: Hazard Example — Sprinkler System
cards.content: Installing a SPRINKLER SYSTEM in the premises DECREASES the risk. A sprinkler system reduces the chance of fire spreading and causes less damage — it is a POSITIVE PHYSICAL FEATURE that reduces hazard and can lead to a DISCOUNT in premium.

cards.title: Sources of Information for Underwriter
cards.content: Valid sources of information for the underwriter: (1) Annual Accounts of Proposer, (2) Pre-Acceptance Risk Survey of the asset, (3) Proposal Form. NOT a source of information: REGISTRATION CERTIFICATE OF INSURER — this document belongs to the insurance company and has no relevance to underwriting a risk.

cards.title: What is a Deductible / Excess Clause?
cards.content: A DEDUCTIBLE (also called EXCESS CLAUSE) is a clause inserted in an insurance policy that requires the insured to bear a fixed initial amount of every loss themselves. The insurer pays only the amount above this threshold.

cards.title: Objective of Deductible Clause
cards.content: The PRIMARY PURPOSE of inserting a deductible or excess clause is to ELIMINATE SMALL CLAIMS. Since the insured has to bear small losses themselves, they will not bother filing trivial claims. This reduces administrative costs for the insurer and encourages the insured to be careful.

cards.title: What is No Claim Bonus?
cards.content: NO CLAIM BONUS (NCB) is a reward given by the insurer to the insured when NO CLAIM has been made during the policy year. Example: If a car insured for a year has no accident or claim, the insured gets a discount on the premium at the time of renewal.

cards.title: Importance of NCB
cards.content: No Claim Bonus is a POWERFUL STRATEGY to improve UNDERWRITING EXPERIENCE. It also forms an INTEGRAL PART OF THE RATING SYSTEM. NCB encourages policyholders to avoid small claims and take better care of their insured assets.

cards.title: Warranty in Motor Insurance
cards.content: In motor insurance, one key WARRANTY (condition that must be followed) is: THE VEHICLE SHOULD NOT BE USED FOR SPEED TESTING. This is a condition written into the motor insurance policy. Other options like 'wash daily' or 'not for personal luggage' are not standard warranties.

cards.title: Insured Declared Value (IDV)
cards.content: In motor insurance, the INSURED DECLARED VALUE (IDV) is based on the MANUFACTURER'S SELLING PRICE of the vehicle. It is not the registration price, cost price, or arbitrary price. IDV represents the current market value of the vehicle and is the maximum amount payable in case of total loss.
